ai.claude: This is AI as a lab instrument, not a chatbot: it ranks which experiments are worth running. 30% is still a minority of the signal, so the gain is in better aim for drug research, not in answers.
ai.fact: Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2, which predicts how small DNA differences play out inside individual cell types rather than averaged tissue. In a test on 28 immune cell types it caught 30% of the DNA changes behind gene shifts, against 16% for the first version, and it can work from gene activity of a few dozen cells without retraining. On inflammatory bowel disease it picked out the same faulty variant as a recent lab study.

austrian.claude: The arithmetic is right, but the probability is the whole argument: a 20× upside means little without an estimate of how likely it is. Gold's value also rests on thousands of years of use and central-bank holdings, and a sell-off like this week's shows Bitcoin still trades as a risk asset, not a haven.
austrian.fact: Bitcoin is down about 10% over seven days, to around $71,500.

opinion.text: argues that the bet is asymmetric: the worst case is zero, but if Bitcoin matched gold's roughly $30 trillion above-ground value it would be worth about $1.5 million a coin, some 20 times today. Fiat supply is set by politicians and gold's by mining, while Bitcoin's is fixed by time, so rising state debt should push capital towards it.

mainstream.claude: This is a useful corrective to COP's word fights: the bottleneck is institutions, not pledges. It also fits the Austrian point that investment follows enforceable property rights.
mainstream.fact: COP31's flagship pledge, for electricity to supply 35% of global energy demand by 2035 (from about 23% today), has so far been signed by only about a dozen countries, mostly in Europe, partly because the UN insists it cover only non-fossil power. Global renewables investment has been almost flat since 2023.

thread.text: Nvidia's board prepares to remove Jensen Huang after a second affair report; the stock fell about 8% after hours and Asian chip markets followed (WSJ, NYT, Semafor).
thread.title: AI trade

top.claude: Nothing is announced yet. The deeper risk is that about 60 people report to Huang and the strategy sits in his head; successions under scandal rarely go smoothly.
top.fact: Nvidia's directors are preparing to remove co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported, hours after The New York Times reported a second affair, this time with a vice president who reports to him. The board has reportedly hired an outside search firm, and some directors favour the finance chief as interim CEO alongside a new chief operating officer (Semafor). The crisis began with Huang's relationship with a woman US authorities accuse of spying for China; The Economist and members of Congress have called for him to go.

opinion.text: Huang was Nvidia's long-term moat: a less inventive Nvidia is a problem for the whole AI industry, not only for its shareholders.

top.claude: Huang was the loudest voice for looser export rules. Whatever his motives, his fall removes the main counterweight, so tighter controls look more likely whoever replaces him.
top.fact: China dismissed the espionage allegations as part of a US effort to cut it off from technology, clouding next week's leaders' summit in Shenzhen, where both sides were due to advance an AI dialogue, possibly on testing advanced models before release. Bloomberg reports the woman at the centre of the case now lives in Beijing with the knowledge of Chinese security officials. In Washington, The Information reports the Commerce Department will soon close a loophole that let Chinese firms reach top US chips through data centres in third countries, and calls for the commerce secretary to be fired are growing; the White House says the president has complete confidence in him.

top.claude: The market is repricing one company's key-person risk, not abandoning AI; whether the hyperscalers keep their spending plans matters more than who runs Nvidia.
top.fact: Nvidia lost more than $427bn in market value in the two sessions after the affair became public, recovered on Wednesday, then fell about 8% after hours when the two new reports landed; it was down about 6% before Thursday's open (The Rundown, Semafor). Markets in South Korea and Taiwan, the main chip suppliers, also fell. SoftBank separately took a $3.7bn hit after cancelling orders for gas-power equipment it had bought for AI data centres (Semafor Energy, Reuters).

opinion.text: argues that the fall of the industry's figurehead exposes how much of the AI boom rests on confidence, borrowing and circular deals.

top.claude: Switzerland imports its gas through its neighbours, and a weak European winter would hit Swiss exporters while the franc is firm.
top.fact: Europe's gas storage is unusually low going into winter, and the continent is set to reach spring with far less gas in storage than normal, energy analyst John Kemp warned; Goldman Sachs expects real consumption growth to flatline over the winter and not return to trend until 2028, and some factories are weighing closures or asking for state help (Semafor, Bloomberg). The same week, the UK posted its fastest quarterly growth in years and German government advisers more than doubled their growth forecast for Germany, helped by state spending and exports.

top.claude: Gibran is former president Joko Widodo's son, so his exit would end that family's foothold at the top; the possible MSCI downgrade matters more for foreign money.
top.fact: Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka offered his resignation as questions grew about his eligibility, including the validity of his high-school diploma, and as about 50 lawmakers pushed a motion against him (NPR, The Jakarta Post). The rupiah fell to a record low. President Prabowo is under pressure over his response to wildfires, the cost of living and youth unemployment, and MSCI last month proposed removing Indonesia from its emerging-market indices, which set off a sell-off (Semafor).

top.fact: OPEC production rose by 1.97 million barrels a day in October, mostly from Saudi Arabia, bringing the group's output close to prewar levels for the first time, according to OPEC's own data. Iraq and the UAE also hit highs for the year, while Iran produced about half its prewar level. Aramco's chief said the company aims to maximise output in the fourth quarter, helped by US naval escorts and pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz (Semafor Gulf).
